title: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A graduate student discusses a fossil field trip with a professor.

script.en: Professor, do you have a minute? I'm finalizing the logistics for our summer excavation in Guizhou, and I wanted to check a couple of details with you.
Of course. Sit down. How are things coming along with the permits?

The provincial museum has approved our request, but they've asked us to submit a detailed plan of the sites we intend to dig. That's actually what I want to talk about. The fossil beds we discussed last semester are quite extensive, and I'm not sure how to prioritize them.
Right. The marine deposits there are famous for well-preserved skeletons, but we can't cover everything in one season. What criteria were you thinking of using?
Well, I thought we should focus on the layers that have produced complete specimens in the past. That would give us the best chance of recovering something publishable.

That's reasonable, but don't overlook the less complete material. Sometimes fragmentary fossils tell us more about the ecosystem as a whole. A single spectacular skeleton is nice, but a collection of smaller finds can reveal how species interacted.
I see your point. So maybe we should split the team: one group works the rich layers, and another surveys the surrounding sediments.
Exactly. And make sure someone keeps a detailed record of the stratigraphy at every site. Without that context, even a beautiful fossil loses much of its scientific value.
Understood. I'll revise the plan to include a surveying component and a stratigraphy log. Should I send you the draft by Friday?
Friday works. And one more thing—budget for extra plaster and packing materials. Those specimens are heavier than they look, and we don't want any damage on the journey back.

script.en: Scientists have long assumed that amphibians are creatures of freshwater. Of the more than eight thousand species alive today, none is known to spend its entire life in the sea, and fewer than two percent can tolerate salt at all. This makes a recent fossil discovery in China all the more striking. An international team has described an ancient amphibian, roughly the size of a giant salamander, that appears to have lived entirely in a marine environment. The animal, named Gerrothorax maritimus, had a broad, flattened body covered in bony armor. Its skull structure and heavy plating suggest it was an ambush predator, resting on the seafloor and sucking in prey that came within reach. Researchers compare its hunting style to that of the wobbegong, a carpet shark that uses suction to capture food near the bottom. The puzzle is how an amphibian could survive in salt water at all. Amphibian skin is permeable, allowing water and gases to pass through it; this is useful for breathing and hydration in freshwater, but it leaves the animals vulnerable to salt. The team proposes that the creature's bony armor limited water movement through the skin, while seawater taken in through the mouth was absorbed by the digestive tract and excess salt was removed by the gills. The evidence comes from two exceptionally complete skeletons, dating back nearly 237 million years. Their completeness is itself significant: carcasses that drift at sea usually lose limbs before sinking, but these animals retained their fingers, suggesting they died near where they lived. The finding expands our picture of what amphibians can do and raises new questions about how life adapts to extreme environments.

sections.title: An Amphibian That Made the Sea Its Home
sections.passage: A remarkable fossil discovery in China has revealed an ancient amphibian that appears to have lived entirely in the ocean, a lifestyle no amphibian alive today is known to adopt. The animal, named Gerrothorax maritimus, had a broad, flattened body protected by bony armor and was roughly the size of a giant salamander. Researchers believe it spent much of its life on the seafloor, waiting to ambush passing prey. The discovery comes from an international team at the University of California, Davis, Peking University, and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. Their findings, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, are based on two exceptionally well-preserved skeletons dating back nearly 237 million years to the Late Triassic period. The completeness of the specimens is itself significant: carcasses that drift at sea usually lose limbs before sinking, but these animals retained their fingers, suggesting they died near where they lived. The finding is especially surprising because amphibians are generally unable to survive in seawater. Among the more than 8,000 amphibian species living today, none are known to spend their entire lives in marine environments, and fewer than 2% have any ability to tolerate salt. Mammals, reptiles, and birds, by comparison, all include species that can live entirely at sea without relying on land for food or fresh water. Until this discovery, scientists had never identified convincing fossil evidence of an amphibian with the same ability. Gerrothorax maritimus measured nearly three feet long, but its proportions were far different from those of a modern salamander. Rather than having a long, slender body, it was unusually broad and flattened, with a distinctive disc-shaped form. The structure of its skull, together with its heavy armor, suggests that this ancient amphibian was an ambush predator. Instead of actively chasing its meals, it likely rested on the seafloor until an unsuspecting animal came within reach. "They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in," said Ryosuke Motani, a professor at UC Davis, who noted that the hunting strategy resembles that of the wobbegong, a type of carpet shark that lives near the seafloor and captures prey using suction. The problem comes down largely to amphibian skin. Unlike the relatively waterproof skin of many other animals, amphibian skin allows water and gases to pass through it. This makes it useful for breathing and maintaining hydration, but also leaves amphibians especially vulnerable to the effects of salt water. As a result, modern amphibians generally depend on freshwater habitats or environments close to them. A few species have developed limited salt tolerance, including the crab-eating frog, but even these animals can lose weight when exposed to brackish water and must eventually return to freshwater to recover. Researchers suggest that its extensive bony armor restricted the movement of water through its skin. This protective covering may have reduced its dependence on absorbing water directly through the skin, allowing the animal to take in seawater through its mouth instead.

long_sentences.en: "They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in," said Motani, who noted that the hunting strategy resembles that of the wobbegong, a type of carpet shark that lives near the seafloor and captures prey using suction.

"It's probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what's different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky." The structure of its skull, together with its heavy armor, suggests that this ancient amphibian was an ambush predator.

"We've been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian, and it's a sort of very unusual member of the lineage." The finding is especially surprising because amphibians are generally unable to survive in seawater.
